findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG, ORBICULARIS OCULI

Indication: Bilateral ptosis; neuromuscular junction assessment

TECHNIQUE: Voluntary activation, concentric needle, 20 fibre pairs

RESULTS:
  Mean consecutive difference (MCD): 62 us [reference <35 us] ABNORMAL
  Fibre pairs with increased jitter: 16 of 20
  Blocking: 22% of fibre pairs

CONCLUSION: Markedly increased jitter with blocking, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Abnormal SFEMG of orbicularis oculi: mean MCD 62 us (reference <35 us), increased jitter in 16 of 20 pairs, blocking in 22%. Consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular junction transmission.

action_criteria.label: Measure vital capacity, mouth pressures and cough
action_criteria.rationale: He is breathless on one flight of stairs with fatigable palatal weakness; respiratory muscle strength decides the level of monitoring and whether IVIG or plasma exchange is needed before surgery (20/30/40 rule, Lawn 2001).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 12.4 nmol/L and blocking antibody 62%; MuSK not detected; normal TSH and free T4.
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fatigable ptosis, ophthalmoparesis and palatal weakness with an anterior mediastinal mass: AChR antibodies are the first test, and thyroid function excludes coexisting thyroid disease (Jacob 2025; Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 20% in orbicularis oculi, 17% in nasalis and 12% in trapezius, without post-exercise facilitation.
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation including facial and trapezius muscles
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms a postsynaptic transmission defect and its generalized distribution, and the absence of facilitation argues against LEMS (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MRD1 improves by 3.5 mm on the right and 3 mm on the left after 3 minutes of ice.
action_criteria.label: Perform an ice pack test on the ptotic lids
action_criteria.rationale: A bedside test of neuromuscular ptosis that separates MG from CPEO and other fixed ptosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Well-defined 4.4 cm uniformly enhancing anterior mediastinal mass without invasion, lymphadenopathy or calcification: thymoma most likely.
action_criteria.label: Order CT of the mediastinum with contrast
action_criteria.rationale: The radiograph shows an anterior mediastinal opacity and thymic imaging is indicated in every patient with MG; the CT characterises the mass and plans its resection (Wolfe 2016; Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Increased jitter with blocking in orbicularis oculi.
action_criteria.label: Order single-fibre EMG
action_criteria.rationale: Not needed once RNS shows a decrement and AChR antibodies are positive; an extra study, not an error.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General guidance on thymoma and MG management.
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on thymoma-associated MG
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step.

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.

Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.
Do not start chemotherapy for a presumed lymphoma or germ cell tumour without tissue; a well-defined anterior mediastinal mass with AChR-positive MG is a resectable thymoma until proven otherwise.
required_recommendations: Refer to thoracic surgery for thymectomy with complete resection of the thymoma (indicated for any thymoma regardless of age or MG severity), with WHO histological classification and Masaoka-Koga staging of the specimen.
Give IVIG 2 g/kg over 2 to 5 days or plasma exchange before surgery, because of respiratory muscle weakness (MIP -38 cmH2O, weak cough) and palatal fatigue.
Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three to four times daily and titrate to effect (usually up to 60 mg four to five times daily).

Monitor respiratory function serially (vital capacity, MIP, cough) while weak and around surgery; escalate to high-dependency care if FVC falls below 20 mL/kg, MIP is weaker than -30 cmH2O or MEP falls below 40 cmH2O.
Plan anaesthesia for MG: reduced-dose non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers with quantitative train-of-four monitoring, and postoperative ventilatory monitoring.
If symptoms persist, add prednisone at a low dose titrated upward, with a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT testing) if long-term treatment is needed.

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic event; EEG does not inform a neuromuscular junction disorder.
CSF has no role in myasthenia gravis (Jacob 2025); normal reflexes and gait give no reason to look for Miller Fisher syndrome.
Contrast CT stages a well-defined thymoma without invasion or adenopathy; FDG-PET is not part of the work-up of MG or of a resectable thymoma.
No cardiac symptoms or signs; CT shows no pericardial effusion or cardiac invasion.
Normal ECG and no palpitations or syncope; no arrhythmia question.

accepted: Thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive, generalized (MGFA Class IIb)

differential.key_features: Cannot be excluded before histology, but the mass is well defined and uniformly enhancing without invasion, necrosis, lymphadenopathy or metastasis, and paraneoplastic MG is typical of thymoma.
No lymphadenopathy, no B symptoms; MG with AChR antibodies points to a thymic epithelial tumour.
Age 68; no fat, calcification or cystic component on CT.
Five-month course, fatigable palate, positive ice pack test, RNS decrement and AChR antibodies; CPEO is slowly progressive over years and non-fatigable.
Ptosis rather than lid retraction, no proptosis, normal TSH and free T4.
Non-smoker, preserved reflexes, normal baseline CMAPs without post-exercise facilitation, AChR antibodies positive.
Fatigable, ice-responsive ptosis and palatal fatigue with an RNS decrement; pupils spared; no long-tract signs.

key_clinical_evidence: Five months of bilateral ptosis and ophthalmoparesis with fatigable palatal elevation and exertional breathlessness, without limb weakness.
AChR binding 12.4 nmol/L with a 3 Hz decrement in facial and trapezius muscles and no facilitation: generalized AChR-positive MG (MGFA class IIb).
A well-defined 4.4 cm enhancing anterior mediastinal mass without invasion: thymoma-associated MG, an indication for thymectomy at any age.
Reduced MIP (-38 cmH2O), MEP (64 cmH2O) and a weak cough: respiratory muscle weakness that calls for pre-operative IVIG or plasma exchange and serial monitoring.

findings.description:
CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

Indication: Anterior mediastinal opacity on chest radiograph; bilateral ptosis and ophthalmoparesis

TECHNIQUE: Multi-detector CT chest with IV contrast, 1mm reconstructions, mediastinal and lung windows

FINDINGS:
ANTERIOR MEDIASTINUM:
  Well-defined, lobulated, oval soft-tissue density mass in the anterior mediastinum, predominantly right-sided, measuring 4.4 × 3.2 × 3.8 cm. The mass has homogeneous soft-tissue density (40 HU pre-contrast, 95 HU post-contrast with uniform enhancement). No calcification, cystic component, fat component, or necrosis. The mass partially obliterates the retrosternal space and abuts but does not invade the right atrial border or great vessels. No pericardial effusion.

PLEURAL SPACES: No effusion. No pneumothorax.

LUNG PARENCHYMA: No consolidation, masses, or ground-glass opacities.

LYMPH NODES: No pathologically enlarged mediastinal or hilar lymph nodes.

BONES: No lytic or sclerotic lesions.

IMPRESSION:
1. Well-defined anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass (4.4 cm), uniformly enhancing without fat or calcification, abutting the right cardiac border without invasion. Appearance is most consistent with thymoma (WHO classification pending histology). Thymic carcinoma and lymphoma are in the differential but less favored given absence of adenopathy and homogeneous enhancement.
2. No pleural, pericardial, or pulmonary metastatic disease.

labs.interpretation: AChR binding antibody 12.4 nmol/L and AChR blocking antibody 62% (elevated). MuSK antibody not detected. TSH and free T4 within reference range. AChR antibodies are found in most patients with generalized myasthenia gravis; clinical correlation recommended.

results.finding: Consensus guidance recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma, and any patient with a thymoma should undergo thymectomy. IVIG or plasma exchange may be used before surgery when bulbar or respiratory weakness is significant.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122

results.finding: In the MGTX trial thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.
results.source: Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522

myasthenia gravis thymoma management.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders 2016; update Narayanaswami 2021) recommends AChR antibody testing first, electrodiagnostic confirmation and chest CT or MRI in all patients to detect thymoma; a thymoma is an indication for thymectomy, with IVIG or plasma exchange beforehand when bulbar or respiratory weakness is significant. MGTX (Wolfe 2016) showed benefit of thymectomy in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral eyelid drooping and double vision with breathlessness on exertion

family_history: No family history of neuromuscular or autoimmune disease

social_history.note: Retired teacher; non-smoker; social alcohol use; widower; independent in all ADLs prior to this presentation

patient.history_present_illness:
A 68-year-old British man with no significant prior medical history presented to the neurology ward with a 5-month history of bilateral eyelid drooping and double vision. He first noticed right upper eyelid ptosis that gradually progressed to complete closure over approximately 10 days, followed 6 weeks later by left-sided ptosis and periorbital puffiness. Both eyes exhibited restricted extraocular movements in all directions. He also reported shortness of breath when walking a short distance; he was previously able to walk a mile without difficulty but now dyspneic after climbing one flight of stairs. He denied diplopia at rest (as vision was fully obstructed by ptosis), dysphagia, difficulty chewing, or limb weakness. There was no history of hypertension, diabetes, or malignancy. He had no smoking history and took no medications. His family history was unremarkable for neuromuscular or autoimmune conditions.

On examination, there was complete bilateral ptosis with restricted extraocular movements in all planes. Palatal elevation fatigued on sustained phonation. Limb strength was 5/5 throughout with preserved reflexes and sensation. Auscultation revealed mildly decreased breath sounds at the right base. A chest radiograph performed in the emergency department showed an oval, well-defined radio-opaque lesion in the right hemithorax adjacent to the anterior mediastinum. The radiograph was flagged by the radiographer, and the admitting team initially considered lymphoma or a germ cell tumor.
